questions.stem: The main purpose of preparing budgeted accounting reports is to:
options: prove that the General Ledger balances at the end of the period
report the business's actual profit to the Australian Taxation Office
plan future activities and provide a benchmark for judging actual performance
record the transactions of the past period in the General Journal
questions.explanation: Budgets estimate future cash flows, profit and financial position so the owner can plan, and actual results can later be compared with them in variance reports. Recording past transactions and checking the ledger are the jobs of the journal and the Trial Balance.

questions.stem: Budgeted reports are prepared on the basis that the business will keep trading through the budget period. Which accounting assumption does this apply?
options: the going concern assumption
the accounting entity assumption
the accrual basis assumption
the period assumption
questions.explanation: A budget plans for future trading, which only makes sense if the business is expected to continue, the going concern assumption. The accrual basis governs how revenue and expenses are measured in the Budgeted Income Statement, not whether the business will continue.

questions.stem: The owner of Kookaburra Cycles prepares a Budgeted Cash Flow Statement each month to decide whether to arrange overdraft finance in advance. Which qualitative characteristic is most important here?
options: verifiability, because a budget is supported by the past period's documents
comparability, because the budget is compared with other bicycle shops
understandability, because the owner has no knowledge of business activities
relevance, because the information is used to make an economic decision
questions.explanation: Relevant information helps the user make decisions and predict outcomes, which is exactly the role of a cash budget in planning finance. A budget is an estimate of the future, so it cannot be verified from source documents in the way recorded transactions can.

questions.stem: Which item would appear in a Budgeted Cash Flow Statement but NOT in a Budgeted Income Statement?
options: expected interest on the business loan
planned cash drawings by the owner
expected depreciation of shop fittings
expected wages for sales staff
questions.explanation: Drawings are a cash outflow but not an expense, so they appear only in the cash budget, as a financing item. Depreciation is the opposite: an expense with no cash flow, so it appears only in the Budgeted Income Statement.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Cycles expects accounts receivable of $12,000 at 1 July, credit sales of $66,000 including GST during July, and accounts receivable of $15,000 at 31 July. What are the budgeted receipts from accounts receivable for July?
questions.explanation: Receipts are opening receivables plus credit sales less closing receivables: $12,000 + $66,000 − $15,000 = $63,000. Reversing the opening and closing balances gives $69,000.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Cycles expects accounts payable of $8,000 at 1 July and $10,000 at 31 July, and credit purchases of inventory of $44,000 including GST during July. What are the budgeted cash payments to accounts payable?
questions.explanation: Payments are opening payables plus credit purchases less closing payables: $8,000 + $44,000 − $10,000 = $42,000. Reversing the opening and closing balances gives $46,000.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Cycles collects 25% of each month's sales in that month, 60% in the next month and 15% in the month after. Sales are: May $36,000, June $40,000, July $44,000. What are the budgeted cash receipts from sales in July?
questions.explanation: July receipts are 25% × $44,000 + 60% × $40,000 + 15% × $36,000 = $11,000 + $24,000 + $5,400 = $40,400. Assuming all of July's sales are collected in July gives $44,000, which ignores the credit terms.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Cycles has $5,000 in the bank at 1 August, budgeted receipts of $63,000 and budgeted payments of $70,000 for the month. What is the budgeted bank balance at 31 August?
options: an overdraft of $7,000
a positive balance of $12,000
an overdraft of $2,000
a positive balance of $2,000
questions.explanation: The month's net cash flow is −$7,000, so $5,000 − $7,000 leaves the account $2,000 overdrawn. The $7,000 is the net outflow for the month, not the closing balance.

questions.stem: The Budgeted Cash Flow Statement shows a cash shortfall in September. Which strategy would most directly address it?
options: offering customers longer credit terms to encourage September sales
increasing the owner's planned cash drawings to cover personal costs
delaying the planned cash purchase of a new display stand until October
recording more depreciation on the existing shop fittings in September
questions.explanation: Postponing a cash outflow for a non-current asset moves it out of the shortfall month. Depreciation involves no cash, and longer credit terms delay receipts, which makes the shortfall worse.

questions.stem: Where does the budgeted repayment of loan principal appear in the Budgeted Cash Flow Statement?
options: investing activities
it does not appear, as it is not an expense
financing activities
operating activities
questions.explanation: Repaying borrowed money changes the business's financing, so principal repayments are a financing outflow. They are a cash flow even though they are not an expense, so they appear in the cash budget but not the Budgeted Income Statement.

questions.stem: Which item would appear in a Budgeted Income Statement but NOT in a Budgeted Cash Flow Statement?
options: the planned purchase of a workshop tool for cash
expected doubtful debts on credit sales
expected cash sales of bicycles
a planned capital contribution by the owner
questions.explanation: Doubtful debts are an expense with no cash payment, so they appear only in the Budgeted Income Statement. A capital contribution and a cash purchase of a tool are cash flows that are not revenue or expenses, and cash sales appear in both.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Cycles expects net sales of $120,000 and a gross profit margin of 35%. Other expenses are budgeted at $30,000. What is the budgeted net profit?
questions.explanation: Budgeted gross profit is 35% × $120,000 = $42,000, and deducting $30,000 of other expenses leaves $12,000. The figure of $42,000 is gross profit before the other expenses.

questions.stem: Budgeted cost of goods sold is $78,000. Kookaburra Cycles wants inventory of $20,000 at the end of the period and expects to start with $16,000. What purchases of inventory (excluding GST) must be budgeted?
questions.explanation: Purchases must cover the cost of goods sold plus the increase in inventory: $78,000 + $20,000 − $16,000 = $82,000. Reversing the opening and closing inventory gives $74,000.

questions.stem: In a Budgeted Balance Sheet, the closing bank balance is taken from:
options: the Budgeted Income Statement
the previous period's Trial Balance
the variance report for the previous period
the Budgeted Cash Flow Statement
questions.explanation: The Budgeted Cash Flow Statement starts with the opening bank balance, adds receipts and deducts payments, giving the closing balance for the Budgeted Balance Sheet. The Budgeted Income Statement measures profit, which differs from cash.

questions.stem: The owner's capital is $70,000 at the start of the year. Budgeted net profit is $28,000 and planned drawings are $24,000. What closing capital appears in the Budgeted Balance Sheet?
questions.explanation: Closing capital is opening capital plus net profit less drawings: $70,000 + $28,000 − $24,000 = $74,000. Ignoring the drawings gives $98,000.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Cycles' Budgeted Income Statement shows a net profit of $18,000, but its Budgeted Cash Flow Statement shows the bank balance falling by $6,000. Which plan best explains the difference?
options: an expected decrease in accounts receivable of $10,000
a cash purchase of a $20,000 van and $9,000 of loan repayments
depreciation of $8,000 and an inventory write-down of $4,000
a $15,000 increase in accounts payable during the year
questions.explanation: Buying a van and repaying loan principal use $29,000 of cash without being expenses, so cash falls despite the profit. Depreciation, write-downs, rising payables and falling receivables all make cash higher relative to profit, not lower.

questions.stem: In a variance report, a favourable variance for an expense means:
options: the actual expense was more than the budgeted expense
the actual expense was exactly the same as the budget
the expense was paid in cash rather than on credit
the actual expense was less than the budgeted expense
questions.explanation: For expenses and cash payments, spending less than budgeted is favourable because it improves profit or cash. For revenue and cash receipts the reverse applies: more than budgeted is favourable.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Cycles budgeted sales of $50,000 for March, but actual sales were $46,000. How is this shown in the variance report?
options: $4,000 unfavourable
$4,000 favourable
$96,000 unfavourable
8% favourable
questions.explanation: Actual revenue fell $4,000 short of the budget, which reduces profit, so the variance is unfavourable. A revenue variance is favourable only when actual revenue exceeds the budget.

questions.stem: Budgeted wages were $20,000 and actual wages were $22,500. What is the variance?
options: $42,500 unfavourable
$2,500 unfavourable
$2,500 favourable
$22,500 unfavourable
questions.explanation: Actual wages exceeded the budget by $2,500, so profit is lower than planned and the variance is unfavourable. A higher-than-budgeted expense is never favourable for profit, though there may be a good reason for it.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Cycles' variance report shows Sales $12,000 favourable and Cost of Goods Sold $7,200 unfavourable. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
options: The business paid much more for each bicycle than it had budgeted.
The business should cut its purchases to remove the unfavourable variance.
The unfavourable variance means that profit was lower than budgeted.
More bicycles were sold than budgeted, so cost of sales rose with volume.
questions.explanation: Selling more units naturally raises cost of goods sold, and here the extra gross profit is $4,800, so the unfavourable cost variance reflects higher volume rather than poor control. Profit was higher than budgeted, not lower, because sales rose more than costs.

questions.stem: Budgeted receipts from accounts receivable were $30,000 but actual receipts were $33,000. Which is the most likely reason for this favourable variance?
options: customers paid their accounts faster than expected
customers took longer than expected to pay their accounts
the business bought more inventory on credit than planned
the business recorded more doubtful debts than planned
questions.explanation: Higher-than-budgeted receipts from customers suggest faster collection, perhaps through settlement discounts or follow-up of overdue accounts. Doubtful debts and credit purchases do not involve cash receipts from customers.

questions.stem: Advertising was budgeted at $5,000 but actual advertising was $2,000, a $3,000 favourable variance. Sales were $15,000 unfavourable. What should the owner conclude?
options: The sales variance is favourable because less was spent on advertising.
The saving on advertising may have contributed to the shortfall in sales.
The favourable advertising variance shows that the business was well managed.
Advertising and sales are unrelated, so each variance is judged separately.
questions.explanation: Variances should be analysed together: cutting advertising saved $3,000 but may have cost much more in lost sales. Judging each variance in isolation could reward a decision that reduced profit overall.

questions.stem: A variance report comparing actual with budgeted figures for each of the last six months shows the wages variance growing more unfavourable every month. This is best described as:
options: an adverse trend that the owner should investigate
a one-off variance that is likely to correct itself
a favourable trend, because the business is growing
a limitation of the accrual basis of accounting
questions.explanation: A variance that worsens consistently over several periods is a trend, suggesting the budget or the wage costs need attention. A one-off variance would appear in a single month only.

questions.stem: Which financial indicator measures liquidity?
options: net profit margin
cash flow cover
debt ratio
return on assets
questions.explanation: Liquidity is the ability to meet short-term debts as they fall due, which cash flow cover measures by comparing operating cash flow with current liabilities. The debt ratio measures stability, and return on assets and net profit margin measure profitability.

questions.stem: Which financial indicator measures stability?
options: gross profit margin
asset turnover
debt ratio
working capital ratio
questions.explanation: Stability is the ability to meet debts and continue operating in the long term, which the debt ratio shows through the share of assets financed by liabilities. The working capital ratio is a short-term liquidity measure.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Cycles budgeted a gross profit margin of 35%, but the actual margin was 31%. Which is the most likely cause?
options: Rent for the shop rose more than expected during the year.
The business paid more interest on its loan than expected.
Office wages rose because an extra administrator was hired.
The business discounted its selling prices to clear old stock.
questions.explanation: Gross profit margin depends only on net sales and cost of sales, so price discounting reduces it directly. Rent, interest and office wages are other expenses, which affect net profit margin but not gross profit margin.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Cycles' return on assets rose from 12% to 15%, while net profit was unchanged. What could explain this?
options: The business increased its selling prices and earned a larger profit.
The business borrowed more money to fund higher inventory levels.
The business sold surplus equipment and reduced its average total assets.
The business bought a new van and increased its average total assets.
questions.explanation: With net profit unchanged, return on assets can only rise if average total assets fall, as when surplus assets are sold. Buying a van or borrowing to hold more inventory would raise total assets and lower the return.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Cycles' working capital ratio is 2.4:1, but its quick assets ratio is 0.6:1. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Much of its current assets is inventory, so it may struggle to pay debts quickly.
It holds too much cash, which should be invested in more inventory.
Its long-term debt is too high, so its stability is poor.
Its profit is too low, so it cannot earn enough on its assets.
questions.explanation: A healthy working capital ratio with a weak quick assets ratio means most current assets are inventory or prepayments, which cannot quickly be turned into cash. Stability and profitability are measured by other indicators, such as the debt ratio and return on assets.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of using budgeted reports to make decisions?
options: They can only be prepared for one month at a time.
They must show the same figures as the previous year's reports.
They are based on estimates that may prove inaccurate.
They cannot include any non-cash items such as depreciation.
questions.explanation: Budgets rely on predictions of sales, costs and timing, so decisions based on them are only as good as the estimates. A Budgeted Income Statement does include non-cash items like depreciation, and budgets can cover any period.

questions.stem: The owner of Kookaburra Cycles compares its net profit margin with that of a large national bicycle retailer. What is the main limitation of this comparison?
options: The comparison breaches the entity assumption, so it is not allowed.
Differences in size, location and accounting methods may explain the gap.
Net profit margin cannot be calculated for a small business at all.
Ratios can only be compared with the business's own budgeted figures.
questions.explanation: Comparing with another business is useful, but differences in scale, buying power, location and methods such as depreciation can make the ratios misleading. Inter-firm comparison is not prohibited; it simply needs to be interpreted with care.

questions.stem: Why should non-financial information be considered alongside budgeted and historical reports?
options: Factors such as customer satisfaction and staff skills affect future performance but are not shown in the reports.
The reports can only be prepared after the owner has collected non-financial information from customers.
Non-financial information replaces the need to calculate any financial indicators for the business.
Non-financial information is required by the Australian Taxation Office for every trading business.
questions.explanation: Accounting reports record only what can be measured in dollars, so information such as customer complaints, staff turnover or supplier reliability fills in what the numbers cannot show. It complements financial analysis rather than replacing it.

questions.stem: Which strategy would most directly improve Kookaburra Cycles' net profit margin without changing its gross profit margin?
options: buying bicycles in bulk to earn a larger trade discount
reducing electricity costs by installing more efficient lighting
negotiating a lower purchase price for bicycles from suppliers
raising the selling price of every bicycle by 5%
questions.explanation: Lower electricity costs reduce other expenses, raising net profit as a share of sales while leaving gross profit unchanged. Cheaper purchases, higher prices and bulk trade discounts all work through gross profit, changing the gross profit margin as well.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Cycles needs a new workshop machine but has poor liquidity. Which way of acquiring it would least harm its liquidity?
options: financing it with the bank overdraft repayable on demand
paying for it using cash collected from customers this month
financing it with a five-year loan repaid in instalments
paying the full price in cash from the business bank account
questions.explanation: A long-term loan spreads the cost over several years and adds mostly non-current liabilities, so current assets and liabilities are least affected. Paying cash reduces current assets and an overdraft increases current liabilities, both weakening liquidity.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Cycles' debt ratio has risen to 70%. Which strategy would most directly improve its stability?
options: the owner contributing $30,000 of capital and using it to repay the loan
borrowing $30,000 more to buy inventory for an expected sales increase
converting the bank overdraft into a long-term loan of the same amount
taking larger drawings so the owner can pay off a personal credit card
questions.explanation: Repaying debt with new capital reduces liabilities without reducing total assets used in the business, so the debt ratio falls. Converting an overdraft into a loan changes only the timing of the debt, which helps liquidity but leaves the debt ratio unchanged.

questions.stem: Which spreadsheet use best supports decision-making about a planned price rise?
options: modelling budgeted profit and cash under several possible price and sales levels
recording each actual sale in the General Journal as it occurs
printing last year's Income Statement for the owner to read
checking that the ledger balances before the year-end reports
questions.explanation: Financial modelling lets the owner compare the likely results of different scenarios before deciding, which is the study design's use of ICT in budgeting. Recording and checking past transactions does not show the consequences of a future decision.

questions.stem: Which graph would best compare budgeted and actual sales for each month of a year?
options: a single column showing the year's total variance
a pie chart of the year's total expenses
a clustered column graph with budget and actual side by side
a single pie chart of the year's total sales
questions.explanation: Placing budgeted and actual columns side by side for each month makes the monthly variances easy to see. A pie chart shows parts of a whole at one point and cannot compare two series over time.

questions.stem: To improve profit, the owner of Kookaburra Cycles plans to cut casual staff hours so heavily that customers wait a long time for repairs. Which consideration should the owner weigh most against the cost saving?
options: the entity assumption, which prevents any change to wages
the period assumption, which requires wages to stay the same each year
the social effect on staff and the likely loss of customers' goodwill
the effect on the debt ratio, which would rise as wages fall
questions.explanation: Cutting hours reduces income for staff and may drive customers away, a social and financial cost that can outweigh the saving. Lower wages do not affect the debt ratio, and no accounting assumption fixes wage levels.

questions.stem: The owner prepares an optimistic budget showing strong cash flows to support a loan application, though she expects actual results to be much lower. What is the main ethical concern?
options: The budget understates profit, so the lender will lend too little money.
The budget is too detailed, so the lender cannot understand it.
The budget deliberately misleads the lender about the risk of the loan.
The budget breaches the period assumption by covering too long a period.
questions.explanation: A budget given to a lender should be an honest estimate; inflating it to win a loan misleads the lender about the business's ability to repay. It could also leave the business with debts it cannot service, harming the owner as well.

questions.stem: Kookaburra Cycles can source cheaper bike parts from a supplier that dumps its waste in a nearby creek. Which response best balances the financial and ethical considerations?
options: Switch suppliers, as environmental harm by a supplier never affects a business.
Stay with a responsible supplier and look for savings elsewhere in the business.
Switch suppliers, because profit is the only consideration in business decisions.
Switch suppliers, but record the parts at the old higher cost to hide the saving.
questions.explanation: The study design asks owners to weigh environmental and social considerations as well as profit, and a supplier's pollution can also damage the business's reputation. Recording a false cost would breach faithful representation as well as being dishonest.

questions.stem: A Budgeted Income Statement shows that a new product line will raise profit, but the Budgeted Cash Flow Statement shows that the bank will be overdrawn for six months while inventory is built up. What should the owner conclude?
options: The cash shortfall can be ignored, because profit is the only measure of business performance.
The budgets are inconsistent, because profit and cash must always move in the same direction.
The product line may be worth pursuing, but finance must be arranged to cover the cash shortfall.
The product line should be rejected, because a business can never be overdrawn for any period.
questions.explanation: Profit and cash differ in timing, so a profitable plan can still create a temporary cash shortage that must be financed. Ignoring the cash budget risks being unable to pay debts, while rejecting a profitable plan outright ignores the ways a shortfall can be managed.
